analogy.p: Think of the C=C double bond like a double-hinged door that has been fastened with two latches (the two bonds). One latch is easy to undo, so the door swings open and lets other things through (new atoms bond on). An alkane is like a door that is bolted shut with only single strong bolts: nothing can get in. This breaks down because the double bond is made of shared electrons, not parts that physically swing, and after the atoms add on the carbon atoms are still joined by a single bond rather than the door staying open.

bullets: Alkenes are a **homologous series**: same general formula, similar chemical properties, and a gradual change in physical properties.
General formula: **CnH2n** (for n carbon atoms there are 2n hydrogen atoms).
The functional group is the **C=C double bond**, which controls how alkenes react.
**Unsaturated** = contains a C=C double bond; **saturated** = only single bonds (alkanes).
Alkenes are made by **cracking** long-chain alkanes.
All bonds are **covalent**; each carbon forms **four** bonds in total.
Link: the C=C bond can open up, which is what allows addition reactions and addition polymerisation.
core.p: **Alkenes** are **hydrocarbons** (compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen) that have a **double carbon-carbon bond (C=C)** in their molecules. The double bond is made of two shared pairs of electrons, so each carbon atom in the double bond still forms four bonds in total. Alkenes are **unsaturated** because they contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms. They are produced in cracking and are far more reactive than alkanes, which makes them very valuable raw materials for the chemical industry.

bullets: **Ethene** C2H4: CH2=CH2 (the simplest alkene).
**Propene** C3H6: CH3-CH=CH2.
**Butene** C4H8: for example CH2=CH-CH2-CH3 (but-1-ene); the double bond can also be in the middle (but-2-ene), so there is more than one butene.
**Pentene** C5H10.
Ending **-ene** = alkene; ending **-ane** = alkane.
There is no "methene": at least two carbons are needed for a C=C bond.
Test: if a molecule has formula CnH2n and one double bond, it is an alkene (for example C6H12 is hexene).
Count bonds: every carbon must have four lines around it, and every hydrogen has one.
core.h: The first members: names and formulae
core.p: You must know the first four members of the homologous series: **ethene (C2H4), propene (C3H6), butene (C4H8) and pentene (C5H10)**. The name comes from the number of carbon atoms (eth- = 2, prop- = 3, but- = 4, pent- = 5) with the ending **-ene** to show a double bond. You use the formula CnH2n to work out the molecular formula: for n = 5 the formula is C5H10. You should be able to draw the displayed formulae, making sure each carbon has exactly four bonds and that the double bond is drawn as two lines.

bullets: Ethane C2H6 (alkane, saturated) vs ethene C2H4 (alkene, unsaturated): **two fewer hydrogen atoms** in the alkene.
Alkanes: **unreactive** apart from combustion; alkenes: **reactive** because of the C=C bond.
Alkene vs alkane **bromine water test**: alkene decolourises it; alkane does not.
Both burn: alkenes tend to burn with a **smokier flame**.
Physical properties (boiling point, volatility) of alkenes follow a similar trend to alkanes: longer chain = higher boiling point.
Both are **non-polar covalent molecules** that do not mix with water.
Alkanes are used as fuels; alkenes are mainly used as **chemical feedstock** for polymers and other products.
core.p: An alkane with n carbons has the formula **CnH2n+2** and only single bonds, so it is **saturated**. An alkene has **CnH2n** and a C=C double bond, so it is **unsaturated**. Because there are two fewer hydrogens, the alkene has the capacity to take in more atoms by opening up its double bond. Ethane (C2H6) and ethene (C2H4) show this clearly. Both burn, but only the alkene undergoes addition reactions and decolourises bromine water.

bullets: **Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes** (a specification statement).
The C=C double bond can **break open** so that new atoms can be added to each carbon.
In an addition reaction the **double bond becomes a single bond**.
Only **one product** forms in an addition reaction, so the **atom economy is 100%**.
Alkanes only undergo combustion and substitution under special conditions (not required here).
The double bond is a region of **high electron density**, which attracts reactant particles (extension only).
Link: the same double-bond opening in many ethene molecules makes **poly(ethene)**.
core.h: Why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes
core.p: In an alkane every carbon atom is joined to four other atoms by **strong single covalent bonds**, so there is no easy way for another atom to attach. In an alkene one of the two bonds in the double bond is easier to break, so the double bond can **open up** and each of the two carbons can form a new bond to another atom. This is called an **addition reaction**. The result is a saturated molecule with a single C-C bond. The ability to add atoms across the double bond is what makes alkenes useful as starting materials.

bullets: Reactants: **alkene + hydrogen**; product: the **alkane with the same number of carbons**.
Conditions: **nickel catalyst** and heat.
Ethene: **C2H4 + H2 -> C2H6** (ethane).
Propene: **C3H6 + H2 -> C3H8** (propane).
Butene: **C4H8 + H2 -> C4H10** (butane).
The product is **saturated**, so it no longer decolourises bromine water.
Atom economy is 100% because only one product is made.
Link: the reverse of cracking in terms of hydrogen content.
core.p: Alkenes react with **hydrogen** to form **alkanes**. The hydrogen atoms add across the double bond, so the C=C becomes C-C. The reaction needs a **nickel catalyst** and a raised temperature. This reaction is used in industry to turn unsaturated vegetable oils into saturated fats (as in margarine), where the same type of reaction is used. For ethene the equation is C2H4 + H2 -> C2H6, and for propene it is C3H6 + H2 -> C3H8.

bullets: **Ethene + bromine -> 1,2-dibromoethane**: C2H4 + Br2 -> C2H4Br2.
**Ethene + chlorine -> 1,2-dichloroethane**: C2H4 + Cl2 -> C2H4Cl2.
**Propene + bromine -> 1,2-dibromopropane**: C3H6 + Br2 -> C3H6Br2.
The C=C double bond becomes a **single bond**, and each carbon gains one halogen atom.
Observation with bromine water: **orange to colourless**.
The halogen molecule splits as it adds: Br-Br bond breaks, two new C-Br bonds form.
Only one product, so atom economy is **100%**.
core.p: Alkenes react with **halogens** such as bromine, chlorine and iodine by addition across the double bond. When ethene reacts with bromine, one bromine atom attaches to each carbon and a single product, **1,2-dibromoethane**, is formed. The equation is C2H4 + Br2 -> C2H4Br2. This is the reaction behind the **bromine water test**: the orange colour of bromine disappears because the bromine is used up and the product is colourless. No heat or catalyst is needed for bromine water at room temperature.

bullets: Equation: **C2H4 + H2O <=> C2H5OH** (ethene + steam gives ethanol).
Conditions: **steam, phosphoric acid catalyst, high temperature and high pressure**.
The reaction is **reversible**; unreacted ethene is **recycled** to increase the overall yield.
The product is an alcohol: the OH group is attached to the carbon chain.
Ethanol can also be made by **fermentation**; the hydration route uses a non-renewable feedstock but is fast and gives pure ethanol.
Atom economy of the forward reaction is **100%** because there is one product.
Link: this is the same addition reaction type as with hydrogen and halogens.
core.h: Addition with water (hydration) to make ethanol
core.p: Alkenes can be **hydrated** to make **alcohols**. Ethene reacts with **steam** (water vapour) in the presence of a **phosphoric acid catalyst** at a high temperature (about 300 degrees C) and high pressure (about 60-70 atmospheres) to make **ethanol**. The equation is C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH. The reaction is **reversible**, so not all of the ethene is converted in one pass: the unreacted gases are recycled. This is an important industrial route to ethanol, which is used as a solvent and a fuel.

bullets: Complete combustion: **alkene + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water**.
Ethene: **C2H4 + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 2H2O**.
Propene: **2C3H6 + 9O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O**.
Butene: **C4H8 + 6O2 -> 4CO2 + 4H2O**.
Incomplete combustion gives **carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot)**, for example C2H4 + 2O2 -> 2CO + 2H2O.
Carbon content by mass: ethene 24/28 = 85.7%; ethane 24/30 = 80.0%, so ethene is smokier.
Carbon monoxide is a **toxic gas** that stops red blood cells carrying oxygen (link to Biology and Chemistry).
This is the specification point: alkenes burn with a **smoky flame because of incomplete combustion**.
core.p: Alkenes burn in oxygen in the same way as other hydrocarbons. In a plentiful supply of air they undergo **complete combustion**, producing **carbon dioxide and water**. For example C2H4 + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 2H2O. However, alkenes tend to burn with a **smoky flame** because of **incomplete combustion**, which produces carbon (soot) and carbon monoxide. This is because alkenes have a **higher proportion of carbon** than the matching alkane, so there is not enough oxygen to burn all the carbon to CO2.

bullets: Reagent: **bromine water**.
Alkene: **orange -> colourless** (decolourised).
Alkane: stays **orange** (no change).
The reaction is an **addition reaction**: bromine adds across the C=C double bond.
Shake the mixture so the bromine and the hydrocarbon mix.
Gases can be bubbled through bromine water; liquids can be shaken with it.
The test works for any unsaturated hydrocarbon, not just ethene.
Link: use the same test to show that cracking has produced an alkene.
core.h: The test for alkenes: bromine water
core.p: The standard chemical test to distinguish an alkene from an alkane uses **bromine water**, which is orange (or yellow-brown). Add a few drops of bromine water to the sample and shake. If an **alkene** is present, the bromine reacts across the double bond and the mixture turns from **orange to colourless**. If the sample is an **alkane**, no reaction occurs and the solution stays **orange**. Examiners need the word **colourless**, not "clear", because a coloured solution can also be clear.

bullets: Hydrogenation: alkene + H2 -> alkane (add H2 to the formula).
Hydration: alkene + H2O -> alcohol (add H2O to the formula).
Halogenation: alkene + X2 -> dihaloalkane.
Combustion method: C atoms give CO2; H atoms give H2O (H/2 molecules); oxygen needed = (2 x CO2 + H2O) / 2.
Propene check: C3H6 -> 3CO2 + 3H2O needs 9 oxygen atoms on the right, i.e. 4.5 O2, so double: 2C3H6 + 9O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O.
Butene check: 4CO2 + 4H2O needs 12 O atoms, i.e. 6O2.
Pentene check: C5H10 + 7.5O2 -> 5CO2 + 5H2O, so 2C5H10 + 15O2 -> 10CO2 + 10H2O.
Never change a subscript in a formula to balance an equation; only change the large numbers in front.
core.h: Writing and balancing equations for alkene reactions
core.p: You must be able to write **balanced symbol equations** for the reactions of the first four alkenes. The trick is to treat each reaction type systematically. For addition reactions, the whole of the other reactant is added, so the formula of the product is just the sum of the formulae: C2H4 + Br2 = C2H4Br2. For combustion, balance carbon first (one CO2 per carbon), then hydrogen (one H2O per two hydrogens), and finally count oxygen atoms on the right to find the number of O2 molecules, doubling everything if the number is a fraction. Always recount each element at the end.

bullets: Polymers: **poly(ethene)** from ethene, **poly(propene)** from propene (see the addition polymerisation note).
Alcohols: **ethanol** from ethene and steam (hydration).
Other chemicals: for example dihalogenoalkanes and antifreeze.
Source: alkenes are made by **cracking** long-chain alkanes (catalytic or steam cracking).
Links to bonding: covalent bonding, double bonds, shared pairs of electrons.
Links to rates and equilibrium: the hydration reaction is reversible; a catalyst speeds it up.
Links to atom economy: addition reactions have **100% atom economy**.
Links to sustainability: the supply of alkenes depends on crude oil, a finite resource.
core.h: Uses of alkenes and links to other topics
core.p: Alkenes are used to **produce polymers** and as **starting materials for the production of many other chemicals**. The most important use is **addition polymerisation**: many small alkene molecules (monomers), such as ethene or propene, join together by opening their double bonds to form long chains of poly(ethene) and poly(propene). Alkenes are also used to make ethanol, antifreeze (ethane-1,2-diol) and other chemicals. Because alkenes come from cracking, this topic links crude oil, fractional distillation, cracking, polymers and alcohols together in one chain of reasoning.

bullets: Moles = mass / Mr; mass = moles x Mr.
Mr of ethene C2H4 = 28; Mr of propene C3H6 = 42; Mr of C2H4Br2 = 188 (Br = 80).
Atom economy = (Mr of desired product / sum of Mr of all products) x 100; for one product it is **100%**.
Percentage yield = actual mass / theoretical mass x 100 (always check the units and the ratio).
The equation ratio for ethene + hydrogen is **1 : 1 : 1**, which keeps calculations simple.
Check: the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products: 28 + 160 = 188.
core.h: Atom economy, yield and calculation skills
core.p: Addition reactions of alkenes are efficient because they produce **only one product**, so all the atoms in the reactants end up in the desired product and the **atom economy is 100%**. You may be asked to use the equation to find a mass or a number of moles. The method is: write the balanced equation, convert the given mass into moles using n = mass / Mr, use the ratio from the equation, and convert back to mass using mass = n x Mr. For example 7.0 g of ethene (Mr 28) is 0.25 mol, which can make 0.25 mol (47 g) of 1,2-dibromoethane.

exam: **Describe the test for an alkene** (2 marks): add bromine water, shake; orange to colourless. Never write "clear".
**Define unsaturated** (1 mark): contains a carbon-carbon double bond.
**Name/draw** the first four alkenes: ethene, propene, butene, pentene; draw displayed formulae with four bonds per carbon.
**Explain why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes** (2 marks): they have a C=C double bond that can open up, so other atoms can be added.
**Write equations** for addition with H2, H2O, Br2 (and Cl2), and for combustion; check every atom.
**Explain a smoky flame** (2 marks): incomplete combustion, producing carbon (soot), because alkenes have a higher percentage of carbon.
**Conditions** command: hydrogenation - nickel catalyst; hydration - steam with phosphoric acid catalyst, high temperature and pressure.
**3-4 marks**: compare ethane and ethene (formula, bonding, saturated/unsaturated, bromine water result).
**6 marks**: structure answers as formula and bonding, test, reactions with equations, and uses; link each to the double bond.
**Calculation questions**: use moles = mass / Mr, the equation ratio, then mass = moles x Mr; show every step.
Use the command words: **State** (short fact), **Describe** (what happens), **Explain** (give reasons, use because), **Calculate** (show working).

mistakes.r: Alkenes are unsaturated because they contain a carbon-carbon double bond.
mistakes.w: Alkenes are saturated because they contain hydrogen.

mistakes.r: Alkenes are CnH2n; CnH2n+2 is the general formula for alkanes.
mistakes.w: General formula of alkenes is CnH2n+2.

mistakes.r: Every carbon has exactly four bonds; a double bond counts as two.
mistakes.w: Drawing a carbon with five bonds in propene or butene.

mistakes.r: Alkenes are more reactive because of the C=C double bond, which can open up in addition reactions.
mistakes.w: Alkenes are more reactive because they have more hydrogen atoms.

mistakes.r: They burn with a smoky flame because of incomplete combustion, as they have a higher proportion of carbon.
mistakes.w: Alkenes burn with a smoky flame because they are large molecules or burn badly.

mistakes.r: The double bond becomes a single bond as the new atoms add on.
mistakes.w: In an addition reaction the double bond stays.

mistakes.r: Ethene + steam -> ethanol: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH.
Count O: the right side has 6 O atoms, so 3O2 are needed: C2H4 + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 2H2O.

summary: The specification asks you to know that alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a C=C double bond and the formula CnH2n, to name and draw the first four members, and to describe their combustion and their addition reactions with hydrogen, water and halogens, including the bromine water test. It matters because alkenes made by cracking are the starting materials for polymers and many other chemicals.

terms.d: A hydrocarbon with a carbon-carbon double bond and the general formula CnH2n.
A family of compounds with the same general formula, similar chemical properties and the same functional group.
The atom or group of atoms that gives a compound its characteristic reactions; for alkenes it is C=C.
Containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
A compound consisting of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
Two shared pairs of electrons between two atoms (four electrons in total).
A reaction in which atoms are added across a C=C double bond, so the double bond becomes a single bond.
The addition of hydrogen to an alkene to form an alkane, using a nickel catalyst.
The addition of water (steam) to an alkene to form an alcohol.
The addition of a halogen (for example bromine) across the C=C double bond.
An orange solution used to test for alkenes, which turn it colourless.
Burning in plenty of oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water only.
Burning in limited oxygen to form carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water.
A measure of how much of the mass of the reactants ends up in the desired product.
A small molecule that joins with many others to make a polymer.

worked.ans: Add bromine water to each gas and shake. Ethene, which is unsaturated, decolourises it from orange to colourless because it undergoes an addition reaction, but ethane, which is saturated, does not react so it stays orange.
worked.q: Describe how you would test whether a gas is ethene or ethane, and give the results. (3 marks)
steps: Mark 1: bubble the gas through (or shake it with) bromine water.
Mark 2: ethene turns the bromine water from orange to colourless.
Mark 3: ethane produces no change; the solution stays orange.

worked.q: 7.0 g of ethene (Mr = 28) reacts completely with bromine to form 1,2-dibromoethane, C2H4Br2. Calculate the mass of 1,2-dibromoethane formed. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80) (3 marks)

worked.ans: 2C3H6 + 9O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O. In limited oxygen incomplete combustion occurs, forming carbon (soot) and carbon monoxide, giving a smoky flame, because alkenes have a high proportion of carbon.
worked.q: Propene burns completely in oxygen. Write a balanced equation and explain why propene burns with a smoky flame when the air supply is limited. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 2: with limited oxygen, incomplete combustion happens.
Mark 3: carbon (soot) and carbon monoxide form.
Mark 4: propene has a higher proportion of carbon than propane (36/42 = 85.7% versus 36/44 = 81.8%), so more oxygen is needed to burn it fully.
